clue.text: 22 across use poorly written notes

explanation.surface: A cross-referenced pharmacist makes poor use of something, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poorly' scrambles the ten letters of the 22 across answer plus USE.
explanation.definitionFit: Printed scores are musical notes set down on paper for players to read.

clue.text: Other arrangement supporting strike so far

indicators.note: in a down clue a supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes second
an arrangement of the word other reorders its letters

explanation.surface: Some other plan backs a strike that has gone on until now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' rearranges OTHER into HERTO, which 'supporting' places beneath HIT in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb meaning up to this point in time, a formal synonym of so far.

clue.text: Try hitting net after start of Badminton Cup

indicators.note: the net-cord piece comes after the B

explanation.surface: A racket-sport scene: having a go, clipping the net early in a badminton cup match.
explanation.walkthrough: LET is the tennis call for a serve that touches the net; 'start of' gives B.
explanation.definitionFit: A drinking vessel with a stem, so a kind of cup, as in a trophy or wine glass.

clue.text: Tribe with the magic lantern

indicators.note: the letters come with, that is carried inside, the words magic lantern

explanation.surface: A tribe gathered round an old magic lantern show.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across magiC LANtern.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish family group or kinship group, a close synonym of tribe.

clue.text: Messing up passage, turned to squirming right away

indicators.note: turned here means twisted round into a new order
right going away means the letter for right is dropped from squirming

explanation.surface: Someone garbles a quotation and squirms with embarrassment at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right away' looks like 'immediately' but splits into R and 'away', its deletion signal; 'turned' then rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting a quoted passage wrong is messing it up when reciting it.

clue.text: German approval on the rise of united China is hot stuff

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: people who are united are at one
Cockney rhyming slang: china plate = mate, so a pal

explanation.surface: A German nods approval as unified China becomes a hot property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the rise' reverses ONE PAL to LAPENO. China = pal is Cockney rhyming slang (china plate, mate).
explanation.definitionFit: A Mexican green chilli pepper is spicy food, literally hot stuff.

clue.text: Cub stars?

definitions.meaning: a young ... is a small one
the constellation Ursa Minor, home of the Pole Star

explanation.surface: Young sporting talent described as rising stars.
explanation.walkthrough: Cub stars suggests junior sports heroes, but read as two definitions: a bear cub, and the constellation Ursa Minor.
explanation.definitionFit: A bear cub is a small bear, and the northern constellation Ursa Minor bears the same English name.

clue.text: See 7
Public strip show hit for six when covering election

stripping each of these words takes off its outer letters, leaving the middles

explanation.surface: A striptease act struck out of the ground during an election campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit for six' is a cricket term for a huge blow, pure misdirection here: each word is simply stripped to its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek phrase for the common people, the masses or general public.

clue.text: Comment for the audience from a team with strange ideas

indicators.note: strange suggests the letters are in an odd order

explanation.surface: A remark to the crowd from a team full of odd notions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges IDEAS; 'a team' is a second route too, A plus SIDE (a team).
explanation.definitionFit: A theatrical remark spoken to the spectators, unheard by others on stage.

clue.text: Morning gone, chameleon switches position

indicators.note: the remaining letters switch places with one another
morning being gone means it is removed from the lizard word

explanation.surface: As morning passes, a chameleon shifts where it sits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone' takes AM out of CHAMELEON, leaving CHELEON; 'switches' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: A level or rank in an organisation, a sense of position.

clue.text: See 24
It's a virtue, yet returning to cover it would be daring

indicators.note: if the reversed word covered the answer the result would be the daring word, so that word minus those letters is the answer
returning means the word yet is read backwards

explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' gives TEY; wrapped round the answer (TE ... Y) it makes TEMERITY, daring.
explanation.definitionFit: Worth or excellence; a virtue is a good quality, as merit is.

clue.text: High ebbs and flows, primarily catching nothing

indicators.note: the primary, first, letters of each word are taken

explanation.surface: Tides ebb and flow, and a fisherman catches nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' looks like high tide but means drug-affected. 'primarily' takes E, A, F.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone completely unable to hear catches no sound at all.

clue.text: Diagrams showing Lewis after school holding up one train

indicators.note: the school and author letters hold the reversed pair between them
the author's initials come after the rest

to tame an animal is to train it

explanation.walkthrough: Lewis is the author C. S. Lewis; 'up' turns the one-and-train pair round in this down entry, giving EMATI.

clue.text: Fierce protests arising from company's internal store layout

explanation.walkthrough: 'layout' yields ESTOR, which sits inside; 'company's' supplies the S as well as the business.
explanation.definitionFit: Used figuratively, a blaze of outrage means intense, furious protests.

clue.text: Satchmo's gripe?

parts.note: the trumpeter's nickname is the stomach word with its letters put in disorder

explanation.surface: Louis Armstrong, nicknamed Satchmo, has a complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer as wordplay reads 'STOMACH, in disorder', which gives SATCHMO. 'gripe' looks like a grumble but is a pain in the gut.
explanation.definitionFit: Gripes are sharp bowel pains, an ailment of the gut.

clue.text: What helps one go without head on beer? A pint, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters might be arranged another way
the beer word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A pint of beer with no frothy head might help you go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without head' leaves EER; 'possibly' rearranges EER plus A PINT. 'go' means go to the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A laxative eases bowel movements, helping someone go to the lavatory.

clue.text: A nice end for troubling decades

indicators.note: troubling the words stirs their letters up

explanation.surface: A pleasant conclusion after years of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubling' rearranges A NICE END.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin plural of decennium, a period of ten years.

clue.text: Not on in church to finally lose face for a drink container

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
a light not on is off

explanation.surface: A churchgoer's embarrassment: switching off and losing face at a service.
explanation.walkthrough: CE, the Church of England, is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A large cup for tea or a hot beverage is a drink container.

clue.text: Fnooze party?

parts.note: a nap word with its S turned to F, as snooze becomes Fnooze, gives a festive celebration

explanation.surface: A nonsense word, a sleepy party.
explanation.walkthrough: Fnooze is snooze with S changed to F; do the same to SIESTA, a Spanish snooze.
explanation.definitionFit: A festive celebration in Spanish-speaking countries, made from the afternoon nap by one letter swap.

clue.text: Lots of coal fires

explanation.walkthrough: 'fires' reads as hearths, but it is the verb meaning dismisses.
explanation.definitionFit: Coal comes in big bags, and to dismiss staff is to give them the boot.

clue.text: In clothes? Emperor? Always!

indicators.note: the letters sit in the words that follow

explanation.surface: A nod to the fable of the emperor's new clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across clothES EMPERor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for always, familiar from mottoes like semper fidelis.

clue.text: Scientist's note in box

parts.note: mi is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A researcher's memo filed away in a box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scientist's' reads as scientist is.
explanation.definitionFit: One who studies chemistry is a kind of scientist.

clue.text: Young creature giving rise to endless criticism
